title: Red Sox CEO Sam Kennedy calls season ‘embarrassing,’ but says Craig Breslow’s job is safe
content:
Boston Red Sox CEO Sam Kennedy called the team’s season “embarrassing” during his weekly radio appearance on WEEI on Thursday, noting that if the situation doesn’t improve soon, the team could be sellers at the trade deadline.

However, Kennedy ultimately offered support for chief baseball officer Craig Breslow.

“I think it’s important here at the outset to acknowledge how embarrassing, unacceptable, maddening, frustrating — whatever words you want to use— the past two and a half months have been,” Kennedy told “The Greg Hill Show.” “There’s no way to sugarcoat it. It’s been awful, especially when you consider the stated goal of building upon what happened last season (after reaching the postseason).”

Given the team’s struggles, including a three-game sweep at the hands of the Tampa Bay Rays this week that sent them to 12 games below .500 for the first time since the 2020 season, Kennedy was asked about whether Breslow’s job is safe.

“I fully understand the questions about Craig Breslow and his job security and all of that, but the issue of change there, just to be clear, is not on the table,” Kennedy said. “He is working as hard as anyone to get things back on track.”

When asked why ownership continues to support Breslow, despite their stated disappointment with the club, Kennedy pointed to Breslow’s strengthening of the pitching infrastructure and to the team’s return to the playoffs last season. Yet he made it clear that last place in the American League East is not where they want to be.

While the Red Sox are known to be searching for a right-handed bat, Kennedy indicated time is ticking for the club to remain in the buyer’s market.

“With the passage of time, you have to take an honest assessment and see where you are,” Kennedy said. “At the current moment, there are a lot of discussions going on in terms of improvement and how we get this thing back on track.

“But let’s be honest, unless things change dramatically, we may have to pivot here from what our initial planning was,” he added. “It wouldn’t be responsible to do otherwise. We’re here in mid-June, and we have to see what happens over the next couple weeks, and then we’ll reassess.”

A report earlier this week from ESPN’s Buster Olney indicated a member of the ownership group had been reaching out to clubs on his own to push along potential trade talks.

Kennedy said he assumed the report was the result of being at last week’s MLB owners’ meetings in New York City with John Henry and Tom Werner. He noted various conversations between team owners about their clubs and that any information they get is passed to the front office, but added that “no one is trying to play general manager.”

More than six weeks ago, the Red Sox fired Alex Cora and six coaches after a 10-17 start. In 39 games since, they’ve gone 17-22.

The offense continues to sputter; injuries to Roman Anthony and Garrett Crochet have kept two of the team’s biggest stars off the field and the bright spots on the team are few and far between.

“I don’t remember a period feeling as visceral as it does right now; it’s been awful,” Kennedy said.

Kennedy has been the CEO since 2015, when he took over for Larry Lucchino. He said the current state of affairs is as bad as he remembers it in his 25 seasons with the club, citing only the 2011 and 2012 seasons as more frustrating.

Henry, the principal owner, has made Kennedy the team spokesman and Kennedy said he’s not focused on his own job security as the organization flounders into obscurity.

“That obviously is a question for others,” Kennedy said. “I love this organization, and my job is to set the overall course for the franchise. I’m the CEO and president. I work for ownership; I’m a partner in Fenway Sports Group and work day to day with John and Tom and Mike (Gordon) and all our partners, Theo Epstein, who’s a partner.

“All of us are feeling it. So I don’t think about my job security each and every day, I think about what it’ll take to get better. It falls on all of us, and nobody is free of blame.”
